splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA permits plan actuaries to adopt actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date when calculating employer withdrawal liability. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for the thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be established no later than the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, giving plans flexibility to use the most current data available.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The split affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises fundamental questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to find violations and impose consequences after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend the term beyond what was imposed in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the stricter gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars raising any previously presented claim — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any previously presented claim, in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements. If not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, so they need only meet § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standard for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome could fundamentally reshape how courts evaluate candidate standing and affects rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter election procedures, even before an election takes place.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not automatically have standing to challenge election rules pre-election and must demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury beyond speculative vote dilution.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations (such as Auer/Kisor deference to Sentencing Commission commentary) in criminal sentencing contexts.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity trumps agency deference when construing ambiguous criminal provisions, including Sentencing Guidelines. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while others (including the Third Circuit) have held that deference trumps lenity. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when construing ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that when a Sentencing Guideline is genuinely ambiguous, courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's authoritative interpretation in the commentary, even if it produces a harsher result than the rule of lenity would yield.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision that allows courts to sentence below mandatory minimums. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that all three criteria must be met to disqualify a defendant, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that meeting any one criterion is disqualifying. This affects criminal sentencing outcomes nationwide.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, interpreting the 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on deference to Application Note 1 of the commentary.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which states that 'controlled substance offense' includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses, is entitled to controlling deference under Stinson/Kisor. This affects career-offender sentencing enhancements for defendants whose predicate offenses are inchoate crimes. The Sentencing Commission has since amended the guideline text, but the split affects cases sentenced under the prior version.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the ambiguous guideline and inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so conspiracy does not qualify as a controlled substance offense.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to § 924(c)) may be considered as an extraordinary and compelling reason, or as a factor, for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law when evaluating compassionate release motions. Some circuits hold that such changes can never contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while others permit courts to consider them alone or in combination with other factors. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to authorize this, but some circuits (like the Seventh) have held that amendment exceeds the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute covers a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled. The Eighth Circuit holds that any state-law controlled substance offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling, while other circuits require the substance to be federally controlled. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal scheduling requirement
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes state-law offenses regardless of whether the substance is controlled under federal law, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when imposing revocation sentences, or whether revocation sentences must be oriented solely toward facilitating reentry and rehabilitation.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation sentences may be imposed as punishment for the violation itself. The Sixth Circuit permits courts to expressly punish for supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that the purpose of revocation is to sanction the breach of trust and facilitate reintegration, not to impose additional punishment. Dissenters in the Sixth Circuit have noted this places their circuit at the extreme of the split.

positions.label: Punishment for violation permitted
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences as punishment for violations of supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must focus on breach of trust/reentry
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should be oriented toward sanctioning the breach of the court's trust and facilitating the defendant's reintegration, not imposing punishment for the underlying violation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration) exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether they may use civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens).
splits.description: Since Preiser v. Rodriguez, circuits have been divided on whether habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges to conditions of confinement or only for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement. This longstanding split affects whether federal prisoners can use civil rights statutes to challenge BOP decisions about conditions, placement, and program eligibility, including First Step Act time-credit disputes.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for all confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to any aspect of confinement — including conditions, placement, and BOP program decisions — must be brought through habeas corpus rather than civil rights actions.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive only for fact/duration challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas is the exclusive remedy only for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, while conditions-of-confinement challenges may proceed through civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil appeal deadline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days) applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the appeal deadline. The majority of circuits hold that the civil deadline applies because the fee motion is ancillary to the criminal case, while a minority apply the shorter criminal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view in United States v. Onamuti.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that the civil appeal deadline applies to Hyde Amendment orders because attorney's fee motions are civil matters ancillary to the criminal case, giving appellants 60 days to appeal.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Manchester Farming Partnership

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that the criminal appeal deadline applies to Hyde Amendment orders because the fee motion arises from and is part of the underlying criminal proceeding, giving appellants only 14 days to appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the appreciation in a debtor's property between the original Chapter 13 filing and the good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds it belongs to the estate based on the broad scope of § 541(a), while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor based on the statute's structure and legislative history.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad scope of § 541(a), means post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence — claims that might also be raised in a habeas petition under § 2255 — as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether district courts considering compassionate release motions may take into account claims that a defendant's underlying conviction or sentence was legally flawed, or whether such claims must be channeled exclusively through habeas proceedings under § 2255. This affects the scope of the compassionate release remedy for federal prisoners.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider potential legal errors in the underlying conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Must channel through § 2255
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the validity of the underlying conviction or sentence cannot serve as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release and must instead be raised through habeas proceedings.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
